Port Alpha

The Future of American Shipbuilding

In modern history, every global power has been backed by the power of naval and commercial fleets. American-built ships helped win two World Wars and have sustained decades of deterrence. U.S. leadership in shipbuilding anchored the global order that our economy and alliances depend on.

Today that leadership is eroding. And while America’s fleet shrinks, China’s fleet continues to grow.

Ensuring American leadership in shipbuilding will require a new approach and new infrastructure. This is the purpose of Port Alpha.

The Problem

01

Today, America faces a shipbuilding problem. We no longer have the ability to produce the ships we need at the speed and scale we need them to support the future fleet, protect our seas, or preserve the ability to move and operate across the world’s most important waters.

The numbers don’t lie. In 1999, China held roughly five percent of global shipbuilding capacity. Today it holds more than half,1 operating at 23.2 million tons of annual production capacity against less than 100,000 tons in commercial shipbuilding in the United States.2

In 2024, China launched 1,400 merchant vessels. America launched five.3

1,400Merchant vessels launched by China in 2024
5Merchant vessels launched by the United States in 2024
5%50%+China’s share of global shipbuilding capacity, 1999 vs. today

The People’s Liberation Army Navy passed the U.S. Navy in hull count four years ago, and the gap is widening.4 Roughly 80 percent of global trade moves by sea,5 but the United States builds less than one percent of the world’s commercial ships.

Meanwhile the demand on our shipyards has never been higher. The Navy’s shipbuilding plan calls for a larger fleet that integrates manned and unmanned platforms. The Administration’s Maritime Action Plan, the President’s August 2026 memorandum on rebuilding the Navy and the shipbuilding industrial base, and the SHIPS for America Act all call for a strategic commercial fleet of U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged vessels.

Unfortunately, only eight American shipyards can build a ship over 400 feet and every one of them is fully committed.6 In addition, the industry needs roughly 250,000 skilled workers over the next decade that it does not currently have.7

More money aimed at the yards we already have is necessary. However, it is nowhere near sufficient. You cannot surge a system that has no room left to surge.

Called to protect American interests at sea, Saronic is building Port Alpha: a shipyard committed to building vessels for both defense and commercial applications, at a scale and pace not seen on American shores in generations. We are investing in critical capacity by building a clean sheet shipyard – a shipyard of the future – to reimagine and reinvigorate shipbuilding in America.

Designed to be one of the most advanced shipyards on Earth.

Introducing Port Alpha

02

Port Alpha takes a software-defined approach coupled with global best practices to deliver one of the world’s largest and most advanced shipyards, designed from the ground up for speed and scale. Unlike legacy shipyards which are constrained by inherited layouts built around bespoke vessels with lower production rates, Port Alpha is designed from the ground up to build a variety of vessels at scale, with modularity and throughput defining the facility’s architecture. Port Alpha also leverages strategic partnerships with established shipbuilders, like Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI), to ensure access to the most advanced autonomy-capable maritime systems and technologies possible.

Port Alpha is designed with autonomy in mind, but what makes it work for autonomous vessels — design for manufacturing, linear flow, production automation, and process discipline — works just as well for manned ships. That’s shipbuilding capacity the country can put to work across the board.

After a year-long nationwide search, we chose Brownsville, Texas as the site for Port Alpha. The site offers deepwater access and room to grow for decades. More than $3 billion in planned investment will create up to 10,000 direct jobs, from welders and machinists to engineers and naval architects. Together with the State of Texas, Cameron County, the Port Isabel Independent School District and the Port of Brownsville, we will make South Texas a center of excellence for advanced maritime manufacturing.

Investment & Economic Impact

$3B+Total planned investment
10,000Direct jobs created (up to)
$160BEconomic impact for Cameron County over the next decade

Port Alpha will initially be capable of producing vessels up to 850ft.; future site expansion could support production of vessels over 1,200ft. At opening, Port Alpha will introduce an initial 150,000 gross tons of annual shipbuilding capacity — more than doubling current U.S. commercial shipbuilding capacity — with the potential to scale to over 2 million gross tons. Construction has already begun, targeting initial operations in 2028.

The first vessels built at Port Alpha will be Landing Craft Utility (LCU) vessels under a U.S. Navy contract awarded to Saronic. With 835 acres today and the ability to expand to over 4,000 acres in the coming years, Port Alpha is built to adapt to what the nation needs as a strategic national asset.

Read the Navy announcement

Location & Site

835Acres today, with the option to expand to 4,000+ acres
2,500+Feet of Phase 1 deepwater quay, with the option to expand to 5,000+ feet

But what matters more than dollars and acres is Saronic’s production philosophy. In almost every legacy shipyard, the facility dictates the manufacturing process, rather than the vessel dictating the facility. Yards built around fixed waterfronts and inherited layouts force ships through inefficient material paths, congested work areas, and constant rehandling. The cost is measurable: optimized layouts that minimize rework, handling, and waiting can cut construction cycle times by 30 to 60 percent.8

The world’s best yards closed part of this gap by leveraging modern manufacturing, but they retrofitted those principles onto legacy infrastructure. Port Alpha is a clean sheet design, with every layout, crane, and material path optimized for the vessels and their production rate rather than inherited from precedent.

Whether building to support the urgent needs to deliver the manned vessels of today or building to deliver the autonomous fleets critical to our future success at sea, Port Alpha also incorporates vessel design and automation to introduce multiple efficiencies not found in existing U.S. shipyards.

Facility Layout

Throughput and flow-efficiency targets drive layout, crane coverage, and shop sizing of Port Alpha, and linear, unidirectional flow is built into the footprint while bottleneck risk is engineered out rather than managed after the fact. Early-stage outfitting capability is designed into the yard, with envelopes sized to accommodate a range of vessel classes.

The result is that the steel travel distance falls sharply versus legacy U.S. yards, transport shifts off cranes and onto more efficient modes, and final hull erection consolidates from dozens of complex lifts to a handful of large-block placements, collapsing cycle time at a key constraint point.

Phase 1 Facility Specifications

4M+Square feet of enclosed production space at full expansion
75,000Tonnes (150 million lbs) of steel processed annually in Phase 1; 600,000+ tonnes (1.3+ billion lbs) at full expansion
2–4Build positions for final ship erection
20Ships per year by 2035 (up to)

Vessel Design

For autonomous vessels, and where possible with manned vessels, Saronic designs for manufacturing from day one, with shared structural details, systems, outfitting standards, jigs, cutting programs, and work instructions carrying over from one vessel class to the next. Designing for that repeatability from inception enables robotic welding, digitized quality control, CNC fabrication, and data-driven scheduling to deliver their full return.

Production System

Production runs as a measured, fully integrated ecosystem with statistical process control at every stage. Every workstation is metered for cycle time, throughput, defect rate, and rework, and dimensional measurement catches deviations before they become downstream rework. Material, hardware, and consumables arrive at the workstation pre-kitted to each work order, and weekly plan-reliability and material-readiness gates keep crews from starting work that will stall.

Together these practices attack transport, waiting, and rework that consume significant legacy yard cycle time. Learning is captured in station-level data rather than only tied to a single hull, so gains compound across a mixed orderbook, while the same repeatability accelerates talent development.

Production Capacity

150K+Gross tons of annual capacity in Phase 1 — more than doubling U.S. commercial shipbuilding capacity
1.5–2MGross tons annually at full buildout, with potential to expand 3–5× with additional land
850+Feet maximum ship length (65,000 tonnes) in the initial phase; up to 1,200+ feet at full expansion

With a new approach to facility layout, automation, design and production, Port Alpha will help revitalize America’s defense and commercial shipbuilding base. The shipyards that built Liberty Ships during World War II were commercial yards before the war and returned to commercial production afterwards. Our base vessels are agnostic to end use or end user. The maritime industrial base is more resilient when it can serve defense and commercial customers alike. Designing and building for both markets keeps the workforce, tooling, and production infrastructure continuously active, rather than idle or volatile.

Horizons

03

Port Alpha is ambitious. It needs to be. We are facing a significant shipbuilding gap with China, exacerbated by atrophy in a proud sector of the American workforce and industrial base, exposing us to great economic and geostrategic risk.

Port Alpha is also tremendously exciting. We see that reflected in the support from sailors and Admirals, welders and pipe fitters, draftsmen and naval architects, local and state officials, and maritime operators of all varieties. Our Franklin shipyard is an example of what is possible when you combine manufacturing and engineering talent, private capital, a software-defined approach and conviction. Our 180′ Marauder built out of our Franklin shipyard went from prototype to production in less than one year. This is a proof point that the American industrial playbook of old is still alive. Lead with ingenuity. Turn the unbelievable into the routine. Build what no one else dares to build.

We are privileged to work during an era of renewed national interest in reindustrialization. Our collaboration with local, state, and federal representatives on Port Alpha is proof that shipbuilding has outsized importance for American security. We are honored to support their efforts to secure the future of this vital American industry.

Port Alpha is our calling and our purpose. It is our commitment not just to restore what was, but to deliver what can be. It enshrines an unshakeable belief that American workers can build the most sophisticated maritime systems on Earth. It hails a new era of maritime autonomy, delivered at a scale and cost that will deter conflict and reshape entire industries.

America is a maritime nation.
Let’s build it together.

Port Alpha

The Future of American Shipbuilding

In modern history, every global power has been backed by the power of naval and commercial fleets. American-built ships helped win two World Wars and have sustained decades of deterrence. U.S. leadership in shipbuilding anchored the global order that our economy and alliances depend on.

Today that leadership is eroding. And while America’s fleet shrinks, China’s fleet continues to grow.

Ensuring American leadership in shipbuilding will require a new approach and new infrastructure. This is the purpose of Port Alpha.

The Problem

01

Today, America faces a shipbuilding problem. We no longer have the ability to produce the ships we need at the speed and scale we need them to support the future fleet, protect our seas, or preserve the ability to move and operate across the world’s most important waters.

The numbers don’t lie. In 1999, China held roughly five percent of global shipbuilding capacity. Today it holds more than half,1 operating at 23.2 million tons of annual production capacity against less than 100,000 tons in commercial shipbuilding in the United States.2

In 2024, China launched 1,400 merchant vessels. America launched five.3

5%50%+China’s share of global shipbuilding capacity, 1999 vs. today

The People’s Liberation Army Navy passed the U.S. Navy in hull count four years ago, and the gap is widening.4 Roughly 80 percent of global trade moves by sea,5 but the United States builds less than one percent of the world’s commercial ships.

Meanwhile the demand on our shipyards has never been higher. The Navy’s shipbuilding plan calls for a larger fleet that integrates manned and unmanned platforms. The Administration’s Maritime Action Plan, the President’s August 2026 memorandum on rebuilding the Navy and the shipbuilding industrial base, and the SHIPS for America Act all call for a strategic commercial fleet of U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged vessels.

Unfortunately, only eight American shipyards can build a ship over 400 feet and every one of them is fully committed.6 In addition, the industry needs roughly 250,000 skilled workers over the next decade that it does not currently have.7

More money aimed at the yards we already have is necessary. However, it is nowhere near sufficient. You cannot surge a system that has no room left to surge.

Called to protect American interests at sea, Saronic is building Port Alpha: a shipyard committed to building vessels for both defense and commercial applications, at a scale and pace not seen on American shores in generations. We are investing in critical capacity by building a clean sheet shipyard – a shipyard of the future – to reimagine and reinvigorate shipbuilding in America.

Designed to be one of the most advanced shipyards on Earth.

Introducing Port Alpha

02

Port Alpha takes a software-defined approach coupled with global best practices to deliver one of the world’s largest and most advanced shipyards, designed from the ground up for speed and scale. Unlike legacy shipyards which are constrained by inherited layouts built around bespoke vessels with lower production rates, Port Alpha is designed from the ground up to build a variety of vessels at scale, with modularity and throughput defining the facility’s architecture. Port Alpha also leverages strategic partnerships with established shipbuilders, like Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI), to ensure access to the most advanced autonomy-capable maritime systems and technologies possible.

Port Alpha is designed with autonomy in mind, but what makes it work for autonomous vessels — design for manufacturing, linear flow, production automation, and process discipline — works just as well for manned ships. That’s shipbuilding capacity the country can put to work across the board.

After a year-long nationwide search, we chose Brownsville, Texas as the site for Port Alpha. The site offers deepwater access and room to grow for decades. More than $3 billion in planned investment will create up to 10,000 direct jobs, from welders and machinists to engineers and naval architects. Together with the State of Texas, Cameron County, the Port Isabel Independent School District and the Port of Brownsville, we will make South Texas a center of excellence for advanced maritime manufacturing.

Port Alpha will initially be capable of producing vessels up to 850ft.; future site expansion could support production of vessels over 1,200ft. At opening, Port Alpha will introduce an initial 150,000 gross tons of annual shipbuilding capacity — more than doubling current U.S. commercial shipbuilding capacity — with the potential to scale to over 2 million gross tons. Construction has already begun, targeting initial operations in 2028.

The first vessels built at Port Alpha will be Landing Craft Utility (LCU) vessels under a U.S. Navy contract awarded to Saronic. With 835 acres today and the ability to expand to over 4,000 acres in the coming years, Port Alpha is built to adapt to what the nation needs as a strategic national asset.

But what matters more than dollars and acres is Saronic’s production philosophy. In almost every legacy shipyard, the facility dictates the manufacturing process, rather than the vessel dictating the facility. Yards built around fixed waterfronts and inherited layouts force ships through inefficient material paths, congested work areas, and constant rehandling. The cost is measurable: optimized layouts that minimize rework, handling, and waiting can cut construction cycle times by 30 to 60 percent.8

The world’s best yards closed part of this gap by leveraging modern manufacturing, but they retrofitted those principles onto legacy infrastructure. Port Alpha is a clean sheet design, with every layout, crane, and material path optimized for the vessels and their production rate rather than inherited from precedent.

Whether building to support the urgent needs to deliver the manned vessels of today or building to deliver the autonomous fleets critical to our future success at sea, Port Alpha also incorporates vessel design and automation to introduce multiple efficiencies not found in existing U.S. shipyards.

Facility Layout

Throughput and flow-efficiency targets drive layout, crane coverage, and shop sizing of Port Alpha, and linear, unidirectional flow is built into the footprint while bottleneck risk is engineered out rather than managed after the fact. Early-stage outfitting capability is designed into the yard, with envelopes sized to accommodate a range of vessel classes.

The result is that the steel travel distance falls sharply versus legacy U.S. yards, transport shifts off cranes and onto more efficient modes, and final hull erection consolidates from dozens of complex lifts to a handful of large-block placements, collapsing cycle time at a key constraint point.

Vessel Design

For autonomous vessels, and where possible with manned vessels, Saronic designs for manufacturing from day one, with shared structural details, systems, outfitting standards, jigs, cutting programs, and work instructions carrying over from one vessel class to the next. Designing for that repeatability from inception enables robotic welding, digitized quality control, CNC fabrication, and data-driven scheduling to deliver their full return.

Production System

Production runs as a measured, fully integrated ecosystem with statistical process control at every stage. Every workstation is metered for cycle time, throughput, defect rate, and rework, and dimensional measurement catches deviations before they become downstream rework. Material, hardware, and consumables arrive at the workstation pre-kitted to each work order, and weekly plan-reliability and material-readiness gates keep crews from starting work that will stall.

Together these practices attack transport, waiting, and rework that consume significant legacy yard cycle time. Learning is captured in station-level data rather than only tied to a single hull, so gains compound across a mixed orderbook, while the same repeatability accelerates talent development.

Production Capacity

With a new approach to facility layout, automation, design and production, Port Alpha will help revitalize America’s defense and commercial shipbuilding base. The shipyards that built Liberty Ships during World War II were commercial yards before the war and returned to commercial production afterwards. Our base vessels are agnostic to end use or end user. The maritime industrial base is more resilient when it can serve defense and commercial customers alike. Designing and building for both markets keeps the workforce, tooling, and production infrastructure continuously active, rather than idle or volatile.

Horizons

03

Port Alpha is ambitious. It needs to be. We are facing a significant shipbuilding gap with China, exacerbated by atrophy in a proud sector of the American workforce and industrial base, exposing us to great economic and geostrategic risk.

Port Alpha is also tremendously exciting. We see that reflected in the support from sailors and Admirals, welders and pipe fitters, draftsmen and naval architects, local and state officials, and maritime operators of all varieties. Our Franklin shipyard is an example of what is possible when you combine manufacturing and engineering talent, private capital, a software-defined approach and conviction. Our 180′ Marauder built out of our Franklin shipyard went from prototype to production in less than one year. This is a proof point that the American industrial playbook of old is still alive. Lead with ingenuity. Turn the unbelievable into the routine. Build what no one else dares to build.

We are privileged to work during an era of renewed national interest in reindustrialization. Our collaboration with local, state, and federal representatives on Port Alpha is proof that shipbuilding has outsized importance for American security. We are honored to support their efforts to secure the future of this vital American industry.

Port Alpha is our calling and our purpose. It is our commitment not just to restore what was, but to deliver what can be. It enshrines an unshakeable belief that American workers can build the most sophisticated maritime systems on Earth. It hails a new era of maritime autonomy, delivered at a scale and cost that will deter conflict and reshape entire industries.

America is a maritime nation.
Let’s build it together.

We see that reflected in the support from sailors and Admirals, welders and pipe fitters, draftsmen and naval architects, local and state officials, and maritime operators of all varieties. Our Franklin shipyard is an example of what is possible when you combine manufacturing and engineering talent, private capital, a software-defined approach and conviction. Our 180′ Marauder built out of our Franklin shipyard went from prototype to production in less than one year. This is a proof point that the American industrial playbook of old is still alive. Lead with ingenuity. Turn the unbelievable into the routine. Build what no one else dares to build.
      - paragraph: We are privileged to work during an era of renewed national interest in reindustrialization. Our collaboration with local, state, and federal representatives on Port Alpha is proof that shipbuilding has outsized importance for American security. We are honored to support their efforts to secure the future of this vital American industry.
      - paragraph: Port Alpha is our calling and our purpose. It is our commitment not just to restore what was, but to deliver what can be. It enshrines an unshakeable belief that American workers can build the most sophisticated maritime systems on Earth. It hails a new era of maritime autonomy, delivered at a scale and cost that will deter conflict and reshape entire industries.

Team

We’re a defense technology company led by veterans, technologists, and world-class engineers.

Leadership

  • Dino Mavrookas
    Co-Founder and CEO

    Dino Mavrookas is Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer at Saronic Technologies, where he spearheads the company's strategic vision, product roadmap, and overall performance.

    With eleven years of experience as a Navy SEAL, including eight combat tours, Dino possesses a firsthand understanding of the critical role advanced military technology plays in protecting and empowering U.S. and allied forces.

    Prior to co-founding Saronic Technologies, Dino honed his expertise in private equity at Vista Equity Partners, leading technology investments across various sectors, including government, cybersecurity, finance, energy, and media.

    Beyond his business endeavors, Dino's commitment extends to The Navy SEAL Foundation, where he actively contributes as a board director, providing unwavering support to SEALs and their families.

    LinkedIn
  • Rob Lehman
    Co-Founder and CCO

    Rob is Co-Founder and Chief Commercial Officer at Saronic Technologies, where he leads Growth and Program Execution. He brings diverse experience across 22 years in the Marine Corps and a civilian career spanning multiple defense primes, leading small businesses, and advising companies across the defense ecosystem.

    Upon leaving active duty in 2006, Rob transitioned to the United States Marine Corps Reserve, where he served until retiring in 2024. In the private sector, Rob supported multiple Navy and Marine Corps programs at both Northrop Grumman and ManTech International. As CEO of TTI, a maritime advanced technology supplier, he led the design and delivery of technologies that are afloat on multiple surface combatants today.

    Most recently, Rob led 9 Line Solutions, a government relations and consulting firm he co-founded to help technology companies navigate the DoD acquisition process. He is an inaugural member of the Department of War’s Science and Technology Innovation Board and serves on the National Capital Council of the Navy League of the United States.

    Rob holds a BA in International Politics from Penn State University.

    LinkedIn
  • Vibhav Altekar
    Co-Founder and CTO

    Vibhav Altekar is Co-Founder and Chief Technology Officer (CTO) at Saronic Technologies, where he drives the development of the company's autonomous systems and software architecture. He leads Forward Deployed Engineering, Product, and Special Programs as well as Software, working with cross-disciplinary teams spanning perception, navigation, machine learning, command and control, and systems integration.

    Vib is a highly accomplished perception engineer, with expertise in the field of autonomous systems and maritime technology. He has spent a large part of his career in industry driving advancements in U.S. Department of Defense technology. As one of the earliest engineers at Anduril, Vib lead engineering efforts across multiple programs. His other career highlights include software engineering at Twitter, Juicero, and 8VC.

    In addition to software, Vib provides meaningful thought leadership at Saronic, and invaluable strategic vision for its technological advancements. Outside of Saronic, he seeks opportunities to give back to the entrepreneur community, often through angel investing, advisorship, or teaching classes.

    Vib studied Electrical Engineering at the University of California, Davis. In his free time, Vib likes to play poker, basketball, and cricket.

    LinkedIn
  • Doug Lambert
    Co-Founder and COO

    Doug Lambert is Co-Founder and Chief Operating Officer (COO) at Saronic Technologies where he is responsible for shaping and executing Saronic's operational strategy. He oversees R&D, Engineering, and Production and works closely with Supply Chain and Services leadership to ensure alignment with customer requirements and production timelines.

    Doug has been at the forefront of maritime engineering since 2012, and is a dynamic and innovative engineering leader with a proven track record of turning concepts into reality. As Head of Engineering at Liquid Robotics, Doug was instrumental in the development of nautical robotics, including the Wave Glider and deep sea buoyancy engines. Subsequently as VP Engineering at Terradepth, Doug successfully architected, prototyped and demonstrated a novel diesel electric autonomous underwater vehicle.

    Doug holds a BS in Electrical Engineering from Lehigh University and a Masters of Engineering Management from Dartmouth.

    LinkedIn
  • Patrick DePriest
    Chief Financial Officer

    Patrick DePriest serves as Chief Financial Officer at Saronic Technologies, where he leads financial strategy and capital planning, overseeing FP&A and accounting to support disciplined growth and long-term value creation.

    With nearly 20 years of experience across corporate finance and high-growth technology companies, Patrick brings a deep understanding of how rigorous financial execution and strategic capital allocation enable organizations to scale responsibly and execute on their mission. Prior to joining Saronic, he served as Chief Financial Officer at Merlin Labs, where he led financial planning, strategic initiatives, and operational finance for autonomy programs supporting both commercial and defense applications.

    Patrick holds a BA in Economics and an MS in Accounting from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, as well as an MBA from Boston College.

    LinkedIn
  • Soo Cho
    Chief People Officer

    Soo Cho is the Chief People Officer at Saronic Technologies, having joined the company in July 2025. She leads the company's people strategy, culture, and organizational development, bringing nearly two decades of experience in employment law, people operations, and executive leadership.

    Prior to joining Saronic, Soo served as Chief Operating Officer at Merlin, helping to scale operations and build internal systems. Before Merlin, she spent more than eight years at Palantir Technologies, first as Employment Counsel and later as Head of People, where she oversaw global employment matters and people initiatives.

    Earlier in her career, Soo practiced employment law at Seyfarth Shaw LLP and at Fenwick & West LLP, where she managed complex employment litigation, compliance matters, and client counseling.

    Soo earned her Juris Doctor from the USC Gould School of Law and holds a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from the University of California, Berkeley.

    LinkedIn
  • Tobi Young
    General Counsel

    Tobi Young is the General Counsel of Saronic Technologies. Her responsibilities include managing global legal affairs, regulatory compliance, litigation, risk management, and corporate governance.

    Tobi brings over 20 years of experience with sophisticated legal, regulatory, and compliance issues through leadership roles in all three branches of the federal government and in Fortune 500 companies. Among other governmental positions, she has been an attorney in the U.S. Department of Justice and in the Office of the White House Counsel; a law clerk to U.S. Supreme Court Justice Neil M. Gorsuch; and a press secretary for Congressman J.C. Watts. Tobi also currently serves as the Chair of the Nominating and Governance Committee on the Halliburton Board of Directors (NYSE: HAL) and previously was Senior Vice President of Legal and Chief Corporate Affairs Officer for Cognizant Technologies (NASDAQ: CTSH).

    Tobi grew up in Oklahoma and is a proud member of the Chickasaw Nation. She recently became the youngest inductee into the Chickasaw Hall of Fame.

    LinkedIn
  • Blake Brickman
    VP of Government Affairs

    Blake is the VP for Government Affairs at Saronic Technologies. Prior to Saronic, Blake spent five years at 8VC, an Austin-based venture capital firm. Blake is also an attorney and previously served in various roles in government including as Chief of Staff to a United States Senator in Washington, D.C., Chief of Staff to the Governor of Kentucky, and Deputy Attorney General in Texas.

    Blake is a native of Dallas, Texas and a board member at the Cicero Institute, a state-based policy organization that focuses on transparency and accountability in government. He received a B.A in History and Spanish from Vanderbilt University and a J.D. from the University of Kentucky College of Law.

    LinkedIn
  • Jonas Brown
    VP of Programs

    Jonas is the Vice President of Programs at Saronic Technologies, leading program execution, delivery, and lifecycle support across the company's product portfolio.

    He brings nearly two decades of experience across U.S. Navy and industry leadership roles, with responsibilities spanning combatant shipbuilding, autonomous systems, combat system integration, sensor development, and fleet maintenance.

    Jonas holds a B.S. in Business Operations Management from North Carolina State University and an M.S. in Systems Engineering from the Naval Postgraduate School.

    LinkedIn
  • Dave Cascalenda
    VP of Corporate Development

    Dave Cascalenda is VP of Corporate Development at Saronic Technologies, where he leads mergers and acquisitions, strategic partnerships, and long-term corporate strategy. He works closely with cross-functional teams to accelerate Saronic's growth trajectory and drive long-term value creation.

    Prior to joining Saronic, Dave led Corporate Development at Axiom Space, where he supported the company's growth at the intersection of space infrastructure and national security. Before that, he spent ten years as an investment banker advising public and private companies on mergers, acquisitions, and IPOs.

    Most of his career has focused on the defense and national security sector, primarily working with fast-growing technology and engineering businesses. Dave holds a B.A. in Financial Markets from the University of Minnesota Duluth. Outside of work, he enjoys endurance sports, skiing, playing poker, and traveling with his family.

    LinkedIn
  • Sam Lisbonne
    VP of Product

    Sam Lisbonne is VP of Product at Saronic Technologies. Sam leads the Product Management team, which defines Saronic's product roadmaps and sets the direction of future product development, and Special Programs, an advanced prototyping team responsible for exploring new product verticals. Sam also collaborates across business development, engineering, production, and other functions on a variety of strategic projects.

    Prior to Saronic, Sam managed a portfolio of classified programs as the Technical Director for an advanced research and development team in the Navy. He has also worked at the Defense Innovation Unit, Lawrence Livermore National Labs, the Center for Strategic and International Systems, and Kratos Unmanned Systems, among other organizations.

    Sam holds an MS in Engineering For National Security and a BS in Mechanical Engineering with Honors in International Security from Stanford University.

    LinkedIn
  • John Morgan
    Head of Manufacturing

    John Morgan is Head of Manufacturing at Saronic Technologies. John leads the development and execution of the company's production and manufacturing capabilities, and is responsible for scaling vessel manufacturing from prototype through production at scale. He is an experienced advanced technologies leader with a proven track record of rapidly advancing business units from developmental environments to full production lines.

    Prior to Saronic, John spent nine years leading production and manufacturing teams at SpaceX. He led the development of the full production line for the Raptor engine while significantly increasing team headcount, driving efficiencies, and implementing new processes that generated continuous improvement and accelerated the pace of delivery.

    Outside of the office, John enjoys fly fishing and has a long-standing passion for sailing. He has competed in multiple long-distance races on the West Coast including Farr 40 World Championships, California offshore race week and Newport to Ensenada yacht races.

    LinkedIn
  • John Simmons
    Chief Information Officer

    John Simmons is the Chief Information Officer at Saronic Technologies. He previously served as Saronic's Vice President of Mission Services, building and leading the Mission Operations, Training, Support, and Systems organizations that carried the company's autonomous vessels from early deployments to sustained operations.

    John brings a track record of scaling operations through hypergrowth. Prior to Saronic, he led Peloton Interactive through explosive growth as Vice President of Post-Sales Operations, Senior Director of Supply Chain Development, and Senior Director of Service & Support, building the service, systems and supply chain infrastructure that supported the company's expansion into millions of homes. Earlier, he spent more than six years at AT&T in Chief of Staff, Customer Experience, and Corporate Strategy roles, leading transformation initiatives, including post-merger integration following the Warner Media acquisition.

    John holds a bachelor's degree in Environmental Design from the University of Minnesota, a background that grounds his systems-thinking approach to building technology organizations that scale.

    LinkedIn
  • Nick Stoner
    VP of Growth

    Nick Stoner leads Defense Growth at Saronic Technologies, where he focuses on large-scale business strategy across product lines, portfolios, and development efforts, partnering closely with the executive team to transition innovative maritime autonomy capabilities into funded defense programs.

    With over 12 years of experience spanning defense operations, acquisitions, and industry growth strategy, Nick brings a deep understanding of how requirements development, resourcing, and long- term procurement planning enable advanced technologies to scale responsibly and meet mission-critical needs. His background includes launching and executing complex, multi-year procurement strategies that move capabilities from rapid innovation into enduring Programs of Record.

    Prior to joining Saronic Technologies, Nick led Anduril Industries' maritime business development efforts as a Senior Director, where he managed growth initiatives across subsea and surface domains. Earlier in his career, he served as a Navy Special Operations officer, with operational and staff tours supporting the European, African, and Indo-Pacific theaters, including an assignment on the Chief of Naval Operations staff, where he helped develop and direct the stand-up of multiple unmanned Programs of Record as a U.S. Government Resource Sponsor.

    Beyond his professional role, Nick is a former Navy Fleet Scholar, with an MBA from the Haas School of Business at UC Berkeley and a bachelor's degree from the University of California, San Diego. He resides in San Diego, California, hunting beach break barrels and sunny afternoons with his family.

    LinkedIn
  • Goutham Subramanian
    VP of Software

    Goutham is the VP of Software at Saronic Technologies where he leads the software department. Goutham brings software into the product development process – starting from initial product conception, through prototyping, and while designing for production. Goutham works closely with end users and customers to shape product requirements and ensure hardware + software co-design.

    In addition to software, Goutham contributes to Saronic's product roadmap and go-to-market strategy. Software is a core pillar of saronic's corporate strategy and Goutham contributes to shaping the software strategy and executing the direction.

    Goutham holds a B.S. in Electrical Engineering from North Carolina State University. Prior to Saronic, Goutham worked at Anduril Industries, where he was an engineering lead on new product development initiatives. Prior to Anduril, Goutham founded and operated a distributed sensing startup selling to local governments.

    LinkedIn
  • Natalie Wiegand
    VP of Global Expansion & Integration

    Natalie Wiegand is VP of Global Expansion & Integration at Saronic Technologies where she oversees the evaluation and acquisition of Saronic's manufacturing, engineering and operations facilities around the world.

    Natalie is a seasoned people leader with over 10 years of experience in business operations, recruiting, and human resources. Natalie's career has strong entrepreneurship roots, beginning with her being one of the first entrepreneurs to attend Draper University - an entrepreneurship bootcamp run by VC Tim Draper. She then joined Tesla as one of the first members of the Executive Search team, where she contributed to building the early leadership team that played a key role in the company's success story, including scaling the production of the Model S, and launching the Model X and the first Gigafactory in Sparks, NV.

    Following Tesla, Natalie transitioned to venture capital and was Chief of Staff of Capital Factory, where she streamlined operations, was a trusted advisor to the executive leadership team, and facilitated the firm's growth in Austin, Dallas, and Houston. Natalie then served as Capital Factory's Vice President of People, where she led the HR department that scaled the company through significant growth, while prioritizing employee development, well-being, and diversity and inclusion.

    Natalie has a degree in Economics from University of California, Santa Cruz.

    LinkedIn

Our Values

We know what’s at stake when it comes to defense because we’ve seen it first hand. Our mission is to leverage our combined experiences to develop advanced technology that will revolutionize what’s possible in naval warfare.

V/001

One Mission

We are a united team that puts the security and defense of our country and its allies first. We persist with grit and resilience to ensure a future that is safe, prosperous, and free.

V/002

Solutions Driven

We expertly engineer effective and reliable products to meet each partner’s specific mission. Our approach is to prioritize requirements and emphasize simple, intuitive usability. To us, excellence is finding creative solutions to complicated problems.

V/003

Trust Fuels Triumph

We lead with transparency, and address challenges directly and honestly. Our commitment to integrity extends to everyone we engage with, from teammates to partners. We take pride in embracing their goals as our own.

V/004

United We Win

We treat our teammates with kindness and respect, and we cultivate individual growth and accomplishment by prioritizing the success of our team. We celebrate each other and the opportunity to support our service members.
